- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥ 0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; apply downward bias correction, especially after sharp spikes.
- If model shows gradual upward trend but true outcome drops sharply (e.g., >10% drop in 3-5 days), consider mean reversion bias — reduce forecast slope.
- After a strong upward spike in history (e.g., >10% from prior 5-day avg), model often overshoots; cap forecast at 1.5x recent peak or adjust downward by 5-10% if sentiment turns neutral or negative.
- If sentiment is flat (0.00–0.33) for 5+ days, model often underestimates volatility — increase forecast variance or add 2–3% upward buffer.
- When true outcome is significantly below model (e.g., >15% gap), check for policy or event-driven downward pressure — adjust forecast downward by 3–5% if sentiment shows negative or neutral drift.
- If model forecast is flat or slightly rising but true outcome shows strong downward momentum, consider lagged effect — delay forecast adjustment by 1–2 days if sentiment remains neutral.
- For 30-day forecasts, if last 5 days show strong downward trend, model often fails to capture reversal — add 1–2% upward correction if sentiment shifts to positive or neutral.
